title: Where Is My Cash? Metrics, Cash Traps, and Protecting Profit
summary: Profitable on paper, but short on cash? Learn where cash hides, the five numbers every owner should track, and how an 8-week forecast keeps you one step ahead.
body_markdown:
Running a business with a low bank balance is perhaps the most stressful part of entrepreneurship. So if you’ve ever logged into your bank first thing in the morning, not sure which bills you can pay today, this is for you.


In this article, we’ll walk through how to stop managing your business by checking your bank account, spot dangers before they hit, and provide a practical breakdown of how to think about and project cash flow.


The material covered in this article originally appeared in our[Where Is My Cash webinar](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oWC1mZOIvvE) , led by indinero director of accounting Tina Clark and controller Kirstie Stelly.


If you prefer learning in a presentation-style environment, you can access the full replay[here](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oWC1mZOIvvE) or watch below.


## **Profitable on Paper, Short on Cash**


Has this happened to you before?


Say you run a professional services firm, like our B2B marketing client[W.Bradford](https://www.indinero.com/case-studies/w-bradford-b2b-cfo-advisory/) . Business is good. Your P&L shows a healthy margin, revenue is up compared to last year, and the team is booked solid.


Now, you’re moving into the third week of November and payroll ($50,000), loan ($10,000), and credit card payments ($10,000) have to go out soon. That’s seventy grand out the door, but you’re not worried. You’ve got about that amount in the bank, and quite a few invoices due the same week.


Then your biggest client calls. They’re in a cash crunch, and they need to push payment back a month.


Nothing about your business changed. Profit is exactly what it was yesterday, but now you either zero out your bank account or move into December carrying credit card debt you’d rather not have.


We’ll come back to this example in a moment, but first, let’s look at how easily profitable businesses can end up here.


## **Where Is My Cash Hiding?**


The old adage goes, cash is king, and boy is it true.


Profit is an accounting calculation, but cash is what you use to pay your team, vendors, and the IRS. Most of the time they move together, but when they don’t, it’s usually for a handful of predictable reasons:


- **Accounts Receivable:** You want to offer net 30 terms, or even net 60 with larger clients. But you still have to pay your overhead in the meantime. And until an invoice gets paid, you’re effectively giving customers a 0% interest loan.


- **Inventory:** Products sitting on a shelf are cash you can’t spend.


- **Capital Expenditures:** Big purchases, like vehicles or office build-outs, leave the bank all at once but show up on your P&L as small depreciation expenses spread over several years.


- **Debt Service and Taxes:** Loans, credit cards, and tax distributions all drain your bank balance, but aren’t clearly visible on your income statement or P&L.


The trap can run the other way, too. Sometimes cash in the bank isn’t really yours: sales tax you’ve collected but not paid to the local tax authority, withheld payroll tax, or customer deposits for work you haven’t delivered yet. They inflate your bank balance, which is another reason a daily balance check can mislead.


## **The Fix: An 8-Week Rolling Forecast**


Checking your balance every day is like driving by rearview mirror. Cash positions tell you what already happened, but they don’t show payments you approved that haven’t cleared, the quarterly tax payment due next month, or the client who’s about to pay late.


But a rolling forecast? That’s looking at the road ahead.


### **Why a Forecast, Not a Budget?**


Budgets are set once, usually for a year, and age quickly. On the other hand, rolling forecasts move all the time; each time you update, you drop the week that ended and add a new one at the end, so you’re always making decisions on current numbers rather than January’s assumptions.


### **Why Eight Weeks?**


Eight weeks is the sweet spot between foresight and reliability.


It’s far enough out to act on upcoming challenges. If a shortfall shows up five weeks from now, you still have time to adjust staffing, push a vendor payment, or offer a client a minor discount for upfront payment.


However, it’s also short enough to stay accurate. Six months, twelve months, or twenty-four months out is too far for most businesses to reliably make use of.


### **The Value of a Rolling Forecast**


Let’s return to the professional services firm example we began with. Here’s week three of their forecast, with and without the client payment that put a wrench in things.


Knowing a late payment would put your cash balance in the negative doesn’t prevent a client from paying late, but it *does* show you, weeks in advance, that one invoice is all that stands between you and going into the red.


And that’s a risk you can manage, as long as you see it coming.


**Week 3** **Client pays on time** **Client pays late**


Opening cash $55,000 $55,000


+ Client invoice $45,000 $0


– Payroll $50,000 $50,000


– Loan/credit card $20,000 $20,000


**Ending cash** **$30,000** **– $15,000**


### **How to Build a Rolling Forecast**


Forecasting and math can sound intimidating for a lot of people, but it’s not as bad as you might think. For example, perhaps this experience is familiar:


Do you remember when you were first starting your business, and someone suggested you write a business plan? And it felt a bit like a waste of time? After all, you knew what you wanted to do already. It was all in your head.


Then you sat down and did it, and it turned out the hardest part was taking the time to put pen to paper and write it all down? And that, as an added bonus, you could finally *explain* what you wanted to do to other people, and that it was actually worthwhile in the end?


Forecasting is similar. None of the math involved is especially difficult. Organizing it is probably the biggest challenge, and even that gets easy with a good starter spreadsheet (our[cash flow forecasting article](https://www.indinero.com/blog/free-saas-financial-model-template/) will lead you to a great template).


Then, for each week:


1. Start with your opening cash balance


2. Add expected income: cash sales and any receivables you realistically expect to collect that week


3. Subtract expected expenses: payroll, rent, loans, credit card payments, quarterly tax payments, etc


4. The result is your projected balance, which becomes next week’s opening balance


5. Repeat across eight weeks, and update regularly


## **Metrics Every Business Should Know**


Every indinero client gets a dedicated point of contact. For instance, presenter Kirstie Stelly is one of the phenomenal[controllers](https://www.indinero.com/blog/controller-vs-comptroller-vs-cfo/) keeping clients updated by email, phone, and our regularly scheduled monthly review meetings.


One thing we’ve noticed is clients don’t need finance degrees to run healthy businesses, but there *is* a difference between those who know their numbers and those who don’t.


You don’t have to know everything. But these are the five non-negotiables we recommend knowing and checking on a regular basis:


- **Net Profit:** What’s left of revenue after you account for every cost? As a benchmark, we recommend aiming for 10-20%, but this depends on your industry and how long you’ve been in business.


- **Gross Margin:** What’s left after considering *only* the direct cost of delivering your service (without overhead)? Breaking things out individually like this helps identify your best and worst customers, as well as your most and least profitable endeavors.


- **Cash Runway:** If revenue ended tomorrow, how long could you keep paying your team, rent, and bills? Think COVID-era shutdowns, or a fire that closes your building. Insurance helps, but 3-6 months in the bank is a safe range to aim for.


- **Days Sales Outstanding (DSO):** How long, on average, does it take customers to pay you? Divide accounts receivable by credit sales for the period, then multiply by number of days in the period. Rather than judging individual clients, this shows how your customer base pays as a whole.


- **Break-Even:** How much revenue do you need to cover your fixed and variable costs? Every dollar above is profit, every dollar below comes out of cash.


Clients often ask, “What’s a good net margin?”


It varies by industry, but the restaurant sector hovers around 5%, retail and manufacturing at 10%, professional services at 20%, and tech around 25%. Relevantly, margins change as a business grows from $1M revenue to $10M. For a breakdown of how to protect them as you grow, check out our[pricing strategy article](https://www.indinero.com/blog/pricing-strategy/) .


## **Homework: Build Your First Forecast**


Set aside an hour this week, and run three numbers:


1. Your cash runway, in days. How long could you go without another dollar in revenue?


1. Your days sales outstanding, compared to payment terms. If there’s a mismatch, that’s a good place to look for your cash.


2. Your forecast: opening balance, expected income and expenses, plus ending balance for each of the next eight weeks. When is the balance dipping? What happens if your largest invoice comes late?


If at the end your numbers look comfortable, that’s great news. You can plan for 2027 with confidence. But if they don’t, you have a good idea of where to start.
